articleTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant (Conf. Publ. No.295)
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.

articleTitle: Refurbishment and uprating of hydro generators
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: Economic considerations predominantly determine the refurbishment and/or uprating of hydro-electric generators. Many years experience within GEC Large Machines Ltd. indicates that only some 30% of hydro power station kilowatt loss capitalisation arises from the electromechanical equipment. The electrical machine is responsible for about half that; consequently generator refurbishment is generally well worthwhile. The author discusses the ecological and social considerations and the need for a review of the design of hydro plants. The author then discusses the needs for refurbishment of hydro plants, design modifications, condition monitoring, stator core tests, and the El Cid test technique.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Microgovernor-a replacement for existing large steam turbine governing controls
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: Microgovernor is a state-of-the-art design but the author shows how it is suited equally to existing and new turbine installations. Computer power and accuracy are harnessed to provide cost effective custom functions and to provide a novel mechanical interface. The conflict between software customising and governor safety requirements is resolved. The flexibility of microgovernor offers strong benefits in a refurbishment scheme.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The application of digital control to turbine-generators
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: In many instances refurbishment plans require the implementation of more advanced control techniques in order to realise to the full the potential advantages. This applies where the use of turbine following boiler modes lead to a more economic use of fuel or where improved steam admission procedures for the turbine can reduce the overall start-up time. Such improvements almost invariably require the implementation of overall plant control concepts which can only be effected by the adoption of hierarchical, distributed digital control systems. The author discusses the developments and design of electrohydraulic governing systems for turbines including the functions available, operator interfaces, and installations in the UK, Australia, and Canada.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Refurbishment of turbine generators
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: There are two possible strategies which can be applied to the refurbishment of turbine generators: the unit is operated until there is a breakdown or a serious fault is discovered during maintenance, the repair/corrective modification is then applied to all similar units during subsequent planned outages; or, the generator is completely refurbished for a specified extended design life with accompanying technical and commercial assurances. Recently, generating utilities have embarked on the second strategy and the main part of the authors' work concentrates on the scope of work necessary for complete refurbishment. An outline is given of the inspection and analytical methods used in the revalidation of the stator fabrications and rotor forging. The replacement of materials with modern alternatives is discussed and design changes to improve the reliability and flexibility of the unit are also considered.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Liddell Power Station plant improvement study: the refurbishment of AC and DC auxiliary systems switchgear
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: Liddell Power Station is a base-load coal-fired installation of 2000 MW capacity comprising 4*500 MW sets situated in the NSW Hunter Valley, Australia. The age of Liddell, its significant capacity, and its favourable location for fuel sourcing dictated it as a natural choice for a comprehensive life-extension study. The author discusses the AC and DC auxiliary systems switchgear refurbishment. The AC switchgear was of 11 kV, 3.3 kV, and 415 V. The DC switchgear was of 50 V and 110 V. A cost/benefit analysis is given of the refurbishment.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The use of static power convertor equipment to increase the efficiency of operation power station plant
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: The author deals with the particular beneficial uses to which thyristor power convertors can be put in power stations with specific reference to updating existing ones. The most important area is in the supply of feed water to the steam generating boilers and in the control over the air flow in the boiler to achieve the optimum combustion conditions for the fuel. The second area is in the provision of excitation power to the alternators. With the continuing reductions in the price of static power thyristor equipment compared to that of rotating plant it is now economic and, in fact, more efficient to use thyristor convertors to provide the alternator's excitation power as well as to control it. By such means it is also possible for the control to be faster and more precise enabling fault conditions and sudden load application or removal to be coped with more effectively.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Planning the refurbishment of the generating sets at Roseires in the Sudan
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: The study, planning and development of most sources of power to meet future requirements all involve considerable time and investment and the implementation in general involves long construction periods. In parallel with such plans much attention is now being given to the refurbishment of power plants in order to sustain their availability and at the same time to the opportunities available for uprating. Many aspects both economic and technical have to be considered in the refurbishment of generating sets. The author describes the refurbishment of the generating sets at the Roseires Power Station in the Sudan and some of the work planned for the station in future.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Retrofitting of flue gas desulphurisation plant at large power stations
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: It is planned to install flue gas desulphurisation (FGD) plant during the 1990s to remove 90% of the sulphur dioxide (SO/sub 2/) emitted from 6000 MW of the CEGB's existing coal-fired generating plants. The CEGB also plans to install FGD plant at any future coal-fired generating stations. The authors describe the fundamentals of the FGD processes and their suitability for use in England and Wales. They also outline the electrical engineering and economic aspect of the FGD plant that would be installed by the CEGB.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Refurbishment of power station auxiliary switchgear
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: The role of power station auxiliary switchgear has tended to be looked upon as subsidiary to the item of plant to which it is related. As the satisfactory performance of the switchgear is of critical importance to the overall system performance the author argues that the role of the switchgear is an important consideration in power station refurbishment in its own right. Using the example of magnetic air break type switchgear the author discusses the developments, design changes, and the service life in the refurbishment process.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The renovation of the hydroelectric plants in the Italian network
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: The authors examine renovation of hydroelectric power stations which is restricted to work on the hydraulic areas of the stations. They also look at the renovation of electric and mechanical equipment and the re-arrangement of the electric layout and protection and control system in tune with current methods for managing hydroelectric power plants.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Safety related programmable electronic systems: existing and future guidelines
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: In June 1987 the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) published guidelines on programmable electronic systems (PESs) used in safety related applications. The authors provide an overview of the HSE guidelines on PES's. The guidelines are relevant to safety related systems in a power station environment. The authors also provide information on PES guidelines developments taking place within HSE, industry and international standards bodies.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Exchange of conventional type of generator breakers to vacuum breakers in power stations
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: Refurbishing electrical plants may involve use of newly developed equipment in combination with the existing old machinery designed to cope with equipment of earlier design. Generator breakers installed some decades ago might occupy a lot of space, use substantial auxiliary supply of electricity, compressed air etc. and are often costly to maintain with spare parts running out of stock. The modern type of breakers, for instance the minimum oil, SF/sub 6/ and vacuum breakers, are very efficient and offer advantages on costs for installation and maintenance. One main concern is whether their effective current switching ability might cause transient overvoltages deteriorating the insulation of the generator windings. The authors deal with an exchange of the air blast type generator breakers to vacuum breakers in Storfinnforsen hydro power station in Sweden.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The refurbishment of the temperature regulators at Berkeley NPS
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: Berkeley Power Station has two gas cooled, Magnox fueled, nuclear reactors. Each reactor has a set of control rods, whose insertion into the graphite core can be adjusted to control the nuclear fission. Most of these rods are manually controlled, but a limited number form an automatic control system. The authors discuss the refurbishment of the temperature regulators which were 20 years old.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Refurbishment of control, instrumentation and information systems of existing hydro powerplants-a possible procedure of assessment
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: Very old hydro-powerplants are mostly no longer economical because of lower availability, reliability and efficiency; increased maintenance, expensive operation due to staff requirements and noneconomical exploitation of the existing water power. For such plants, modernisation has to be considered for the following reasons: to increase the technical performance and decrease expenditures for operation and maintenance; technical progress and innovation for possible improvements; and to change the external utilisation conditions of the plant. A renewal of a plant can be made by replacing or overhauling the main components such as gates, valves, turbines, generators, transformers and switchgear, by modernising the control, instrumentation and information system, or both simultaneously.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Munmorah Power Station life extension study controls and instrumentation system
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: The Munmorah Power Station is located on the coast of New South Wales, Australia. It is coal-fired and has four generating units with an effective capacity of 300 MW. The author addresses the engineering considerations and results of the Munmorah Power Station control and instrumentation life extension study.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A GEC approach to power generation control and instrumentation refits
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: The authors look at the GEC approach to power generation control and instrumentation refits. Three projects are briefly described: the Hinkley Point A fuelling machine replacement control system; the Hartlepool/Heysham additional fuel storage facilities; and the Berkeley charge face machinery refurbishment.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Refinery power station, re-instrumentation works
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: With the advent of expensive fossil fuel, industrial consumers reviewed their usage to see if alternative fuel sources would be more economic. However, oil companies had little alternative but to continue using oil and gas. Escalating costs did cause them to review losses (gas being flared) and efficiency. The author illustrates the approach that BP oil successfully implemented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: SSEB experience of refurbishment of turbine supervisory equipment
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: Major refurbishment of the turbine supervisory equipment (TSE) schemes have been carried out at Cockenzie and Longannet Power Stations. Measurements of dynamic parameters on the machine are carried out. These include: shaft to cylinder differential expansion, shaft eccentricity, bearing pedestal vibration, shaft speed, thrust bearing wear, pedestal displacement and valve positions.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Refurbishment of turbo alternator rotors and excitation systems in ageing power stations
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: Alternator winding faults are of two types, stator winding faults and rotor winding faults. Rotors and excitation systems begin to show signs of ageing after 20 to 30 years and rotor faults occur rather more frequently than stator faults during the lifetime of a machine. The author describes the experience of CESC Limited, the public utility which supplies electricity to the city of Calcutta, in connection with the protection of rotors, the location and repair of rotor earth faults, the problems which arise and the safeguards which have to be adopted when running a turbo alternator with a repeatedly repaired, and consequently weak rotor. The methods available for the refurbishment of ageing excitation systems using DC machines are also described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Medium size rotating machinery upgrading: design criteria and technologies
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: After some considerations on the expediency of rewinding an old machine, the authors summarize the techniques applicable to medium size induction and synchronous machines, pointing out the problems which may arise and the advantages provided by the new materials and technologies. The advantages derived from an electromagnetic redesign of the machine are also considered. Some specific topics related to the revamping of rotating machines are examined. Specifically, the most recent developments in the field of excitation systems, variable speed drives and diagnostics are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Refurbishment of turbogenerators for plant life extension
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: The need to replace major components of turbine generators depends on their expected reliability over future operating periods. Assessment of the reliability should take account of operating experience for the particular design of generator and of the condition of lead units judged from detailed inspection and NDT testing during overhaul. However, the expected reliability is only one element of the economic assessment. The decision to exchange plant will necessarily be made by the utility, taking account of such external factors as the availability of spare capacity on the system and the cost of operating replacement plant. The authors discuss various aspects of turbogenerators refurbishment concerned with the rotors and stators.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The refurbishment of electrical plant operating in a geothermal power station
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: In 1983, four HP turbogenerators were de-commissioned, after 25 years continuous service, from the Wairakei Geothermal Power Station in New Zealand due to the ongoing decline in geothermal steam pressure. Two of these machines rated at 12 MW have undergone extensive refurbishment to fit them for a new life at the Ohaaki Geothermal Power Station, which is being constructed. The authors outline the steps taken by the Electricity Corporation of New Zealand to assess, test and refurbish the generators, generator exciters, power transformer, circuit breakers and associated electrical auxiliaries from decommissioning at Wairakei to installation and commissioning at Ohaaki. The measures adopted to improve the control and protection of the units for incorporating into a modern unmanned power station are given. Environmental considerations necessary to avoid hydrogen sulphide corrosion of electrical plant are outlined.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Refurbishment of generator/motor units and main transformers at Cruachan Pumped Storage Power Station
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: The North of Scotland Hydro Electric Board's Cruachan Power Station is situated on the shores of Loch Awe in the Scottish Highlands about 100 km north-west of Glasgow. Power station plant life is considered to be typically of the order of 25 years. The station has been in service for more than 20 years, and although the plant has been regularly maintained the considerably more onerous operating regime has taken its toll, and it was recognised that extensive refurbishment of the plant had become necessary. The authors examine the refurbishment of two of the most critical areas of electrical plant-two of the four generator/motor units, and the two generator/motor transformers. They demonstrate that refurbishment is not just a matter of new parts for old. Problem areas have been carefully analysed, extensive redesign carried out, and solutions incorporated during the refurbishment with the aim of achieving a greatly extended plant life.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Upgrade of C.N. Jose Cabrera, Zorita
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: The 160 MWe, pressurised water reactor C.N. Jose Cabrera (CNJC), located at Zorita, approx. 95 km east of Madrid began commercial operation in 1968 and had consistently operated since then with an availability factor in excess of 80%. Over the period mid-1979 to October 1985 an extensive programme was implemented by the plant owners, Union Electrica Fenosa S.A. (UEFSA), to upgrade CNJC, taking cognizance of regulatory requirements and clarifications which had begun to appear in 1974, and which had not been specific elements in the formulation of the original CNJC design and construction criteria. This programme comprised three phases: survey and assessment, conceptual design and detailed design/implementation. The implementation was completed over two periods of approximately nine months, during extended refuelling/maintenance shutdowns in 1982/83 and 1985. The author addresses the electrical changes and additions that were essential aspects in supporting the overall plant upgrade.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The economics of power station refurbishment
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: The economic and financial analysis of a proposal to refurbish a power station is, in principle, no different from the analysis required for any investment decision. The authors concentrate on the factors that distinguish the economics of refurbishment from the economics of new stations. They describe the circumstances in which refurbishment may be beneficial and discuss how the costs and benefits can be evaluated. Particular considerations that apply to developing and industrialised countries are identified and for the latter they discuss implications for refurbishment in view of the privatisation of the UK electricity supply industry.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Assuring the integrity of large electrical machines in a power station refurbishment programme
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: A considerable number of the 500 MW unit fossil-fired power stations, built by the generating boards in the UK in the late 1960s and early 1970s, are at or approaching their design life of 20 years. There are powerful economic arguments for extending the life of these stations to 30 or 40 years, providing the cost of refurbishment to achieve this aim is not excessive. These arguments are being sharpened by the impending privatisation of the electricity supply industry, following which it is expected that a higher return on the capital invested in installed plant will be required. The authors discuss technical arguments for the refurbishment of large electrical machines in power stations. They highlight for operations and maintenance engineers, the criteria which should be applied in a refurbishment programme to decide whether an electrical machine needs to be left alone, refurbished or even replaced.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Planning of plant refurbishment
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: The authors describe four very different types of plant refurbishment planning-three hydro stations which can be classified as mini, small and conventional and one thermal station. The circumstances leading to refurbishment are quite different for each project described, but having made the decision, the route to implementation should be reasonably conventional. The most important ingredient in planning is defining the scope of work. On site inspection and testing is essential as review of operation and maintenance logs and discussions with power house staff can give leads as to what needs to be done. Investment at this stage-including the loss of generation while machines are being inspected-will remove many delays and financial shocks during implementation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Upgrading of existing precipitators to give reduced particulate emissions
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: Many of the Lodge-Cottrell precipitators operating on UK power plants were designed and installed at least 20 years ago to specifications which related collection efficiency to MCR gas volume. The efficiencies ranged from 98.5% to 99.3%. Since the plants were installed, legislative levels for dust emission have been reduced. This has lead to the development of a practical precipitator design improvement programme aimed at meeting current legislation within the existing casing. The casings represent a high proportion of the total plant cost and, provided the required precipitation performance can be attained, this improvement programme represents a very cost-effective upgrade.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Vacuum switchgear meets the needs of power refurbishment
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: Older power stations are now double shifting and life is being extended. It is now necessary as part of the refurbishment programme to replace the switchgear. The author discusses the design of new vacuum switchgear to meet the needs of refurbishment. Various aspects of the design are discussed including the thermal rating, busbars, construction, earthing switch, materials, and testing. The Aberthaw power station refurbishment project is described as an example.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The replacement of nuclear monitoring equipment
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: The safe and efficient operation of the reactor within nuclear power stations is determined largely by the measurement and control of neutron flux and core temperature. These parameters are measured using complex sophisticated electronics, located throughout the station, which has to be replaced due to component obsolescence and more onerous operating requirements. The author discusses the problems associated with the replacement of these equipments against a background of the dual requirements of satisfying the Nuclear Installations Inspectorate (NII) on safety matters while achieving successful installation during the very limited reactor shut down periods.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The effects caused by the refurbishment of power plant automation on the electrical systems
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: The refurbishment of power plant automation causes extensive changes in the electrical systems. The author looks at the effects refurbishment has on control room equipment, power supplies, switchgear and earthing. The refurbishment itself is also described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Refurbishment of control and instrumentation systems in power stations in South Africa
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: There are at present 21 multi-unit coal fired power stations operating in South Africa; this does not include two new power stations under construction each consisting of six units. A program for refurbishing the older power stations is being implemented; one has already been refurbished, a second is in progress, and a minimum of a further eight is being planned. The authors deal with various technical and economical aspects related to refurbishment of power stations in South Africa.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The need for C and I refurbishment for existing power stations
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: The author looks at the participation of controls and instrumentation (C and I) in achieving the objective of beneficial application of retrofitted equipment. Refurbishment of power stations leads to increased efficiency, higher safety factor and increased reliability amongst others.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Control and instrumentation systems in power station refurbishment schemes
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: To sustain the operation of major plant items in a power station during its proposed life-time requires a planned programme of overhaul and maintenance. This is likely to include the replacement or refurbishment of components due to general 'wear and tear', obsolescence, unavailability of spare parts or as a result of modifications elsewhere on the plant. Control and instrumentation (C and I) systems are particularly prominent in these respects usually having a life expectancy less than that expected for major items of mechanical and electrical plant. To offset this however, it is shown that some of the greatest returns on investment can result from the replacement, upgrading or refurbishment of power station C and I systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Total C and I refurbishment of a 4*500 MW coal fired power station for improved flexible operation using a touch screen based control desk
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: The Didcot power station is situated near Oxford and operates four coal fired boiler/turbine units, with a generation capacity of 500 MW per unit. The authors describe the refurbishment of the control and instrumentation (C and I) system using computer based desk technology with touch screens. This improves flexible operation and also saves time.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Static exciter system for large turbo-generators
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: In the summer of 1986, a problem was found which affected a number of similar AC exciters on 300 MW generators in use in SSEB power stations. There was a need to find some way of releasing a first set of exciters for modification which could then be used to start a rolling programme of modifications, while minimising any loss of availability of generation. Unit 4 at Cockenzie power station was chosen as the first to be modified. This is a coal fired 300 MW unit. The author discusses the replacement of rotating exciter system by a static excitation system which gives enhanced performance and lower losses than the original system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The refurbishment, automation and remote control of Tongland Power Station in the Galloway Hydro Scheme
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: The Galloway Hydro Scheme is situated in the South West corner of Scotland and consists of 6 hydro stations linked to the national 132 kV grid and local 11 kV distribution network. The authors describe the refurbishment, automation and remote control of the Tongland Power Station which has 3*11 MW synchronous generators.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: How expert systems can help solve a host of power station operating and maintenance problems
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: The effective management and operational support for power stations is becoming more critical, more costly, and more complex. The power industry has to satisfy increasing demands for power and increasing and justifiable demands for improving plant safety and reliability. This applies for all types of plants, including nuclear plants, and needs to satisfy the complete range of operational, refurbishment and support requirements. There are increasing demands to provide more cost effective services. The author discusses the use of expert systems in solving these management and operational problems in power stations.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Retrofitting of turbogenerators
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: The author discusses several aspects involved in residual life estimation and subsequent retrofitting of turbogenerators. The useful life of individual components depend on the temperature, and electrical and mechanical stresses. The author discusses these factors and then goes on to discuss rotor retaining rings, rotor rewinding, excitation systems, and stator windings.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Examples of hydro generator refurbishment in Ontario Hydro and the CEGB
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: The authors consider the options available when refurbishment of hydro plant is required. Two examples of refurbishment of hydro generator plant are described which cover two different approaches for plant refurbishment. These are the partial or complete re-planting. An example of complete re-planting of a 51.5 MW hydro generator by Ontario Hydro is described, and the partial refurbishment of a 90 MW pump storage generator-motor by the CEGB considered.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A review of electrical plant life extension in the CEGB
publicationTitle: International Conference on Refurbishment of Power Station Electrical Plant, 1988.
abstract: The time to construct a power station in the United Kingdom from initial planning decisions through to first unit commissioning is approximately 9-10 years. Therefore, there is always the problem as to whether if there is a sustained increase in demand and an economic upturn in the country, the necessary consents and construction activity can be made to secure capacity or not. The extension of life of plant is, of course, an option in these circumstances whereby plant scheduled for decommissioning is retained in service for longer than initially planned.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
